title: Intervals
body:
## The mental model
Intervals require an endpoint convention. Closed [a,b] intervals overlap when one starts exactly where another ends; half-open [a,b) intervals do not. Sorting by start turns merging into comparing the next interval with only the final merged interval.

## Worked example
Closed [1,2] and [2,4] merge to [1,4]. But meeting slots [1,2) and [2,4) can use the same room. For event sweeps, tie ordering must reflect the endpoint convention.

## Common mistakes
Updating an output interval that aliases an input array violates a nonmutation contract. Copy interval pairs before merging.

## A rule worth keeping
Decide endpoint semantics and tie-breaking before choosing < versus <=.

## Put it to work
Before opening the related exercise, predict one tiny case on paper, name a boundary where your reasoning could fail, and write the invariant or guarantee you intend to preserve. After testing, compare the observed result with your prediction. Explain a mismatch rather than merely changing the answer.

### Self-check
- [ ] I can explain the worked example without rereading it.
- [ ] I can construct a boundary case and explain its expected behavior.
- [ ] I can name a cost, limitation, or tradeoff of this technique.
- [ ] I can distinguish a practice result from a production guarantee.
